content_units: 20-Minute Knee-Friendly Mobility Plan

This routine is designed for a 67-year-old with mild knee osteoarthritis who wants low-impact movement at home, no equipment, 20 minutes a day, 5 days a week. It emphasizes mobility, leg strength, balance, and gentle conditioning while avoiding jumping and deep squats.
Practical context
- Informational plan only; it does not replace advice from his clinician or physical therapist.
- Because he takes   lisinopril  , slower position changes and good hydration are sensible to reduce lightheadedness risk.
Weekly Home Exercise Schedule
Day   Focus   Main Exercises   Time
Monday   Mobility + gentle strength   March in place; ankle pumps; seated knee extensions; sit-to-stand from chair; standing calf raises; hamstring stretch   20 min
Tuesday   Balance + joint motion   Heel-to-toe standing near counter; side leg raises; standing hip extensions; gentle knee bends; calf stretch; breathing cool-down   20 min
Wednesday   Recovery mobility   Easy walk indoors/outdoors if comfortable; seated heel slides; quad sets; ankle circles; seated hamstring stretch   20 min
Thursday   Strength + balance   March in place; sit-to-stand; side leg raises; calf raises; supported single-leg stance; gentle stretch   20 min
Friday   Mobility circuit   Seated knee extensions; heel slides; hip abduction standing; mini partial squats to chair; walking laps at home; cool-down stretch   20 min
Daily Session Format
Warm-up: 4 minutes
- March in place slowly: 1 minute
- Ankle circles or ankle pumps: 1 minute
- Gentle knee bends holding a counter, only shallow range: 1 minute
- Shoulder rolls and easy breathing: 1 minute
Main exercises: 12 minutes
Use slow, controlled reps. Rest briefly as needed.
Option 1:   Sit-to-stand from a chair     Builds thigh and hip strength for daily function   1-2 sets of 6-10 reps
How to do it
Option 2:   Seated knee extensions     Helps improve knee motion and quadriceps strength   1-2 sets of 8-12 reps each leg
Knee exercise guide
Option 3:   Standing calf raises     Supports ankle strength and walking stability   1-2 sets of 10-12 reps
Arthritis exercises
Option 4:   Side leg raises at counter     Strengthens hip muscles that support the knee   1-2 sets of 8-10 reps each side
Hip support moves
Option 5:   Heel slides or seated heel glides     Improves knee flexibility without impact   8-12 slow reps each leg
Mobility reference
Cool-down: 4 minutes
- Calf stretch at wall: 20-30 seconds each side
- Seated hamstring stretch: 20-30 seconds each side
- Slow breathing
- Easy walking around the room for 1 minute
Safety Tips for Knee OA and Blood Pressure
- Keep pain during exercise in the   mild   range only; a little soreness is acceptable, sharp pain is not.
- Use a sturdy chair or kitchen counter for balance during standing exercises.
- Avoid deep squats, kneeling under load, twisting on the planted knee, and all jumping.
- Move through a comfortable range; smaller motion is fine.
- Start with   1 set   for the first week, then add a second set only if he tolerates it well.
- Wear supportive shoes, even indoors if balance is not perfect.
- Rise slowly from floor, chair, or bed because lisinopril can contribute to dizziness in some people.
- Stop if the knee becomes more swollen or significantly more painful later that day or the next morning; reduce reps next session.
- A useful rule: symptoms should settle back to baseline within about   24 hours   after exercise.
When to Stop and Contact a Clinician
Stop the routine and contact a clinician promptly if he has:
- Chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, fainting, or marked dizziness
- New irregular heartbeat or feeling like he may pass out
- Knee pain that is sharp, catching, or causes the knee to give way
- Noticeable joint swelling, warmth, redness, or pain that lasts more than 24-48 hours after exercise
- Sudden major drop in function, such as trouble walking, standing from a chair, or bearing weight
- Calf swelling, calf pain, or one-sided leg swelling
- A fall, near-fall, or worsening balance problems
- Blood pressure symptoms such as severe lightheadedness, blurred vision, or unusual weakness
